content: HIV, or human immunodeficiency virus, is a virus that specifically targets and weakens the body’s immune system. It is transmitted through certain body fluids, including blood, sexual fluids such as semen, vaginal fluids, and rectal fluids, as well as breast milk. In the early stages of HIV infection, individuals may experience symptoms such as coughing, body aches, headaches, nasal congestion, and a sore throat. These symptoms often resolve on their own and can easily be mistaken for a flu-like illness. However, some individuals may not exhibit any early symptoms and may feel completely healthy. The only definitive way to determine if someone has HIV is through testing. Over time, HIV progressively damages the immune system, making it increasingly difficult for the body to combat infections and other diseases. This can lead to complications such as heart disease, kidney disease, liver disease, and certain types of cancer. If left untreated, HIV infection can progress to AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome), which represents the most severe stage of HIV infection. Individuals with AIDS have severely compromised immune systems, leaving them vulnerable to opportunistic infections—serious infections that typically do not affect healthy individuals. Without treatment, these infections and the progression of the disease ultimately result in death. Currently, there is no effective cure for HIV. However, with early diagnosis and appropriate medical care, HIV can be managed and controlled, allowing individuals to live longer and healthier lives. Travelers are generally at low risk of acquiring HIV unless they engage in high-risk activities, such as having unprotected sex or sharing needles. HIV can also be transmitted through accidental injuries involving contaminated needles or sharp objects, though this is primarily a concern for healthcare workers. In some low-income countries, blood supplies may not be adequately screened, and medical equipment may not be properly sterilized. Travelers receiving medical or dental care in such settings may face a small risk of HIV infection. HIV affects people worldwide, with sub-Saharan Africa being the most heavily impacted region. Other regions significantly affected by HIV include Asia and the Pacific, Latin America, the Caribbean, Eastern Europe, and Central Asia. To prevent HIV, travelers can take several precautions. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), a medication available as a pill or injection, is highly effective when prescribed by a healthcare provider. Before engaging in sexual activity with a new partner, both individuals should discuss their sexual and drug-use histories, disclose their HIV status, and get tested for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. Consistently using condoms during vaginal, oral, or anal sex from start to finish is essential. Travelers should avoid injecting drugs or sharing needles or other devices that can break the skin. If injecting drugs, only use new, sterile syringes and needles. When getting tattoos, piercings, or acupuncture abroad, ensure that a new, sterile needle is used for each procedure. Similarly, if receiving medical or dental care abroad, confirm that the equipment is either unused or properly sterilized. Travelers with HIV should bring enough of their medications to last the entire trip, as not all countries have access to all HIV medications. It is also important to consult a doctor or travel medicine specialist at least four weeks before departure. This is because certain travel vaccines may not be suitable for individuals with HIV, and additional precautions may be necessary depending on the destination.
